domain: Religious Studies / Comparative Religion / Japanese History
topic_summary: Analysis of Shinbutsu-shugo (Shinto-Buddhist syncretism) in Japan from 6th century to Meiji separation (1868), examining whether 1200+ years of institutional coexistence constituted a coherent unified ontology or pragmatic domain partition. The honji suijaku theory claimed kami as manifestations of buddhas, yet persistent separation (shinbutsu kakuri) and functional division (birth Shinto/death Buddhist) suggest incomplete fusion.

key_entities: Honji Suijaku Theory (9th century framework: kami as emanations of buddhas/bodhisattvas)
Ryōbu Shintō (Shingon school: kami as expressions of Dainichi Nyorai cosmic principles)
Sannō Ichijitsu Shintō (Tendai school: kami as Buddhist guardians)
Yoshida Kanetomo (late medieval reversal: Shinto as root, Buddhism as fruit)
Jinguji (Buddhist temples attached to Shinto shrines)
Shinbutsu kakuri (systematic separation of certain kami from Buddhism)
Ise Shrine / Usa Hachiman (early integration sites)
key_claims: Honji suijaku established hierarchical relationship with buddhas as more fundamental than kami
The two religions never fused completely, kept particular identity in tense un-systematized relationship
Born Shinto, die Buddhist — functional domain partition by life stage
No agreement among specialists on exact extent of fusion
Separation after 1868 still only partially complete today
Relationship existed between particular kami and particular buddhas, not between two systems
key_tensions: Ontological unity (honji suijaku) vs persistent institutional separation (shinbutsu kakuri)
Hierarchical subordination (kami as traces) vs reciprocal parity (setting realms on par)
Systematic fusion (jinguji temple-shrine complexes) vs systematic separation (certain kami kept from Buddhism)
Theoretical coherence (Ryōbu/Sannō unified frameworks) vs practical incoherence (un-systematized tense relationship)
key_mechanisms: Honji suijaku interpretive framework: redefines kami as manifest traces of buddha original substance
Jinguji institutional integration: physical co-location of temples and shrines
Meiji shinbutsu bunri: legal separation dismantling 1200-year arrangement
key_absences: No systematic theology reconciling Shinto purity taboos with Buddhist death rituals — domain partition may be structural necessity not choice
No explanation for why Yoshida reversal (Shinto as root) was possible if honji suijaku was ontologically true rather than politically contingent

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The ontological relationship between kami (Shinto deities) and buddhas/bodhisattvas — whether they are unified manifestations of single ultimate reality or separate entities serving different domains
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive authority distributed across Buddhist schools (Shingon, Tendai), shrine lineages, and imperial/governmental power; no single adjudicator; legitimacy grounded in ritual efficacy and institutional accommodation rather than doctrinal consistency

readings.expected_structural_delta: Ontological hierarchy with buddhas as more fundamental; kami cannot exist independently; Buddhism structurally prior despite historical posteriority in Japan

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas are separate entities serving different functional domains (life/purity vs death/impurity)

readings.expected_structural_delta: Functional complementarity without ontological unity; each system retains independent existence; separation is structural necessity not historical accident

readings.commitment: No coherent ontology exists; 1200-year coexistence was un-systematized pragmatic accommodation of institutional power

readings.expected_structural_delta: Apparent syncretism masks incoherent bundle; relationship between particular kami and particular buddhas, not between systems; theoretical frameworks (honji suijaku) are post-hoc rationalizations of political arrangements

axiom_contradictions.basis: Unified manifestation requires ontological dependence (kami cannot exist without buddha ground); domain partition requires ontological independence (each system operates in its domain regardless of the other). No single framework can hold both kami-as-dependent-trace AND kami-as-independent-domain-entity simultaneously.

Unified manifestation requires that honji suijaku describes actual ontological structure; pragmatic accommodation requires that honji suijaku is political rationalization with no ontological truth-value. A framework cannot hold both 'this theory describes reality' and 'this theory is merely convenient fiction' for the same theory.

omegas.description: If honji suijaku described ontological truth (unified_manifestation_reading), how was Yoshida Kanetomo's late-medieval reversal (Shinto as root, Buddhism as fruit) institutionally possible? Reversal feasibility suggests honji suijaku was political arrangement not ontological necessity, supporting pragmatic_accommodation_reading.
